name: Elena Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a private agency on the edge of the city, mostly in the tower blocks and the old terraced streets round the bus depot. I'm on a thirty-hour contract, which is rare, so I know what I'm getting each week. My first call is Mr Okafor, who's seventy-nine and lost his sight, so I make his breakfast, sort his pills and read him his post. Then it's buses and walking between five more people until about two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being useful in a way you can see. Mr Okafor calls me his eyes, which is nice and also a bit much at eight in the morning. What wears me out is the lifts in the tower blocks, because half the time they're broken and I'm carrying shopping up eleven floors. Money's tight, but I share a flat with my sister Abena, so the rent's split and we get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, back to normal. I'm not someone who gets worked up online, so I'd probably just nod along if it came up at the bus stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my job, which is good, but I also stay on the same low pay. I'd still have less than a month saved. The job feels steady, it's the money that doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my thirty hours and finally start the care diploma the agency keeps mentioning, because it comes with a pay rise. I'd keep using the odd AI app when it's useful, like for recipes. I'd try to put fifty pounds a month aside, which I've said every year and never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. Not great, not bad. In a world where AI is just hype, my biggest worry is still a broken lift and eleven floors of someone's shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you get by. What would one bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Abena lost her job at the call centre, I couldn't cover the rent on my own. Or if I got ill and couldn't work for two weeks, there's no sick pay worth talking about. That's what I think about at night, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I ask a chatbot for diabetic recipes for Mrs Dlamini, because her daughter wants her eating better. Once I used it to help write a complaint about the lifts to the council. It wrote it better than I would have.

do: Start the **care diploma** the agency mentions, which comes with a pay rise.
Keep using the odd **AI app** for recipes and letters.
Try to put **fifty pounds** aside every month.

Keep the thirty-hour contract and the same morning calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use AI for the paperwork. I'd probably say carers are lucky for once, because people still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay about my job, but not about the flat. Answering customers is one of the first things AI would take, and that's exactly what Abena does. If she lost her job, I'd be in trouble too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app the agency used for notes once the others had tried it. I'd start saving harder in case Abena's job went, maybe seventy pounds a month. And I'd ask the agency about more hours, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, for Abena more than me. My job is safe because people still need people, but my sister's call centre job pays half our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Abena works at a call centre. How does this picture look for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be worried sick. She's been there four years and she's good, but they're already testing a chatbot for the easy calls. I'd tell her to start looking now, maybe in care, though she'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your own day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. The notes and the rota would go on an app, and maybe the office would ring me less. The cooking and the washing and reading the post to Mr Okafor would be the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government needs to slow it down until people are ready. I'd say it calmly, though, because shouting doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Abena loses her job in 2028 and I lose mine in 2031. That's both of us out of work within three years. I'd be thirty-one and we'd have no savings at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare pound from day one, and we'd move somewhere cheaper, maybe a one-bed we could share. I'd look at jobs where people still want a person, like hospitals or nurseries. And I'd want to see what the government offered before doing anything too drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. My sister loses her call centre job in 2028 and I lose my care job in 2031. That's both of our wages gone in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking AI, then robots three years after. What happens in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get more hours, because the agency would be cutting office staff and pushing everything onto carers. Abena might come and do care with me for a while. We'd keep our heads down and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Okafor about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr Okafor not to worry, that I'd still be coming. I don't know if that's true, but he'd need to hear it. He gets anxious if anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so let's use it sensibly. I'd tell people to start saving and thinking about what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's better. Abena would have three years before her job goes, and I'd have eight. That's time to save and maybe both of us move into something safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the care diploma in the first year, then look at becoming a healthcare assistant at the hospital. I'd use whatever AI tools the agency brought in so I stayed useful. And I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a month once I had the pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but I can breathe. With five years, my sister and I could both get out of the jobs that robots take, if we start the week it's announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does that change much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to make one change properly. Two years is just panic. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Abena still live together in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. It's cheaper, and we look after each other. Maybe one day one of us gets married, but not with all this going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so nobody should panic. I'd also say the government should use that time to train people properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine if I did the sensible things. I'd be forty when the robots come. But Abena's job goes in 2036, so the flat's still a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diploma, then move into the hospital as a healthcare assistant. I'd save steadily, maybe a hundred a month. I'd use AI tools when they came, once I'd seen others use them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but I'm still not relaxed. Ten years is enough for me to change jobs once, carefully, and that's all I'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you be doing by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working at the hospital, I hope, maybe in the elderly ward. Still with people, but with more training behind me. And maybe a place of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this one hopeful for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. If robots did the lifting and the eleven floors of stairs, my knees would thank them. I'd just want to keep the talking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Abena and I would both lose our jobs before we'd saved anything. What would help is help with retraining that pays while you study, and the agency paying a bit more now so we could save. People think carers worry about robots. I worry about the rent if my sister loses her job first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the lifts. Fix the lifts in the tower blocks and half my bad days go away, robots or not.

headlineQuote: People think carers worry about robots. I worry about the rent if my sister loses her job first.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** carer on a rare thirty-hour contract on the city's edge.
She shares a flat and the rent with her sister **Abena**, who works in a call centre.
She uses AI **now and then**, for recipes and a complaint letter to the council.
Her mood follows **both incomes**: uneasy when only Abena's job is at risk, alarmed when both are.
Her plan is one **careful move** into hospital work after a care diploma.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Abena would both lose their jobs before saving anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that covers wages while she studies.
A bit more **pay now** so she could save.
